scenario: AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

In conclusion, while respecting the tradition is crucial, finding a balance through efficiency and engagement can make the ceremony meaningful without excessive length. message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did something wrong by giving my girlfriend advice on how to improve her cooking. We've been together for a while, and when we moved in together, we agreed that she would handle the cooking because she gets home earlier from work. At first, I was really happy about this because I got to come home to a hot meal, which was a big change from when I was living alone and often just ate takeout or something quick. But over time, I noticed that her cooking wasn't up to the standard I was used to. It wasn't terrible, and everything was edible, but it just didn't taste as good as what I was used to. I thought, maybe she doesn't know that there's room for improvement, so I started giving her pointers. I tried to be constructive, telling her things like she used too little salt or too much spice, or that something was a little burnt or undercooked. I also mentioned how I thought the dish could be better next time. I always made sure to eat everything and say thank you, so I didn't think I was being rude about it. But then, when my mom came to visit, I casually mentioned that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend seemed fine with it at the time, even nodding and smiling. But as soon as my mom left, she went ballistic, accusing me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family. She stormed off and hasn't cooked anything for me since. I apologized, saying I was sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom, but it didn't calm her much. Now, I'm wondering if I overstepped by giving her advice, or if she's overreacting. I never complained about her cooking or threw it out; I was just trying to be helpful. I miss her cooking, and I'm not sure what to do now. Is it AITA (Ask if I'm the Asshole) or is my girlfriend just being crazy? Alright, so to break this down, I need to consider a few things. First, the intention behind my actions. I thought I was being helpful by giving her pointers to improve her cooking. I didn't mean to criticize her or make her feel bad. But maybe the way I delivered the advice came across as more critical than helpful, especially in front of my mom. Another thing to consider is the dynamic between us. We've been together for a while, and we've established a routine where she cooks. Maybe she feels that her role in the relationship is being undermined when I give her advice on something she's responsible for. It could be that she feels competent in her role and doesn't appreciate unsolicited advice, especially in front of family. Also, the timing of my mom's visit might have added pressure. Maybe she felt self-conscious about cooking in front of my mom, and my suggestion that my mom could give her advice made her feel even more insecure or embarrassed. I should also think about how I delivered the advice. Even though I tried to be constructive, maybe the way I phrased things came across as more negative than I intended. For example, saying she used too little salt or too much spice could be seen as pointing out flaws rather than offering suggestions. Furthermore, it's possible that she feels that her efforts are not appreciated, and my focus on improvement is making her feel like her current efforts aren't good enough. This could lead to feelings of inadequacy or resentment. On the other hand, I did try to be supportive by always eating everything and saying thank you, which shows that I appreciate her efforts. But maybe the way I gave feedback was still perceived as negative, especially in front of my mom. In terms of whether I'm the asshole or not, it's a bit subjective. I was trying to be helpful, but the way I delivered the advice might have been insensitive to her feelings. It's possible that she feels disrespected or humiliated, especially in front of family, which is a significant social context. To move forward, I think communication is key. I need to have an open and honest conversation with her about how she feels and why she reacted the way she did. I should acknowledge her feelings and take responsibility for any part I played in making her feel bad. It's also important to listen to her perspective and understand her emotions, rather than just focusing on my intentions. In the future, if I want to give feedback, I should consider her feelings and the context in which I deliver it. Maybe I can find a more supportive way to offer suggestions without making her feel criticized. It's also important to show appreciation for her efforts and not just focus on areas for improvement. Overall, while my intentions were good, the way I delivered the advice might have been insensitive, leading to her feeling humiliated and resentful. It's important to balance helpfulness with sensitivity and respect for her feelings and role in the relationship.
